comments.author: j-pb
comments.story_title: Poop: Performance Optimizer Observation Platform
comments.why_zh: 内存布局主导基准测试结果；人们过度相信噪声统计
comments.quote_zh: Emery Berger 有一个很精彩的演讲讲这个 [1]
comments.text_zh: 现在已经没人该这么做基准测试了。在现代计算机上，代码的内存布局对性能影响极大，不把这一变量排除掉就测性能，只会让你白忙一场：你以为自己改进了什么，实际上只是碰巧让编译器把代码挪了挪位置。Emery Berger 有一个很精彩的演讲讲这个 [1]，他们还开发了一个叫 Coz 的因果分析 profiler [2]。分支预测失败对这一点可能多少不太敏感，但那个演讲的核心观点之一就是：人们做了太多“目测统计”，把底层随机过程的方差误当成了真实信号。用 Zig 搭建 Coz 也相当简单。1. [视频] 2. [链接]
comments.text: Nobody should do benchmarking like this anymore. Memory layout of your code has such a big impact on performance on modern computers that measuring performance without removing that variable leads to wild goose chases, where you think you improved something, but in reality you incidentally got the compiler to move the code around a bit. Emery Berger has an excelent talk on this [1], and a causal profiler that they developed called Coz[2]. Branch miss-predicts might be somewhat invariant to that, but still, one of the main points of the talk is that people do too much eyeball statistics, mistaking the variance of the underlying stochastic process with actual signal. Coz is pretty trivial to set up with Zig too. 1. [VIDEO] 2. [LINK]

comments.author: abainbridge
comments.story_title: Algorithms for Modern Hardware
comments.why_zh: 描述由代码和数据对齐变化引起的性能分析噪声
comments.quote_zh: 对代码的改动通常会改变代码和/或数据的对齐方式
comments.text_zh: 我觉得性能分析那一节可以加一段，讲讲这个视频里描述的那类性能分析噪声：[VIDEO] 视频里说的噪声来源是：对代码的改动通常会改变代码和/或数据的对齐方式，而这往往才是测得性能差异的原因，而不是算法的改动。说它是噪声，是因为对代码做不相关的改动可能又会让它变回来。如果我没记错的话，演讲者建议改进编译器/分析器工具，把这些对齐方式随机化，并多次运行基准测试。
comments.text: I think the profiling section could benefit from a section describing the sort of profiling noise described in this video: [VIDEO] The noise source described is that changes to the code typically alter alignments of code and/or data and that is often the cause of the performance difference measured, not the change to the algorithm. The reason this is noise is because unrelated changes to the code might make it change again. IIRC, the speaker suggests improving compiler/profiler tools to randomise these alignments and benchmark many times.

comments.author: moonchild
comments.story_title: C performance mystery: delete unused string constant
comments.why_zh: 被引用作为 causal profiler 的一个例子
comments.text_zh: > 删除这一行代码，可能会对看似无关的性能微基准测试产生巨大影响。有些数字会变好（例如 +5%），有些会变差（例如 -10%）。同一个微基准测试，在一个 C 编译器上可能变快，在另一个上却变慢。这里存在一种根本性的脱节，使人类很难对计算机程序的性能进行推理。因为光速太慢，我们所知的计算机体系结构将始终依赖 cache 和 OoO 来获得高性能。人脑确实似乎是乱序工作的，但它只习惯于思考一个按顺序运行的世界。当我们使用心理理论（theory of mind）时，我们并不是在模拟他人的心智，而是用我们自己的心智作为他们心智的模型；见镜像神经元[1]。因此，标准代码基准测试并不太有用，除非它们能展示数量级的速度提升。即便是像 causal profiler[2][3][4] 这样试图控制性能中易变因素的工具，作用也有限；它无法控制所有变量，而且它的结果很可能会被它试图控制的那种体系结构差异所推翻。相反（就性能而言），我们应该关注三个因素：- 代码可维护性 - 算法复杂度 - 缓存一致性。其他一切都是干扰。1. [LINK] 2. [VIDEO] 3. [LINK] 4. [LINK]
comments.text: > deleting this one line of code can have a dramatic effect on seemingly unrelated performance micro-benchmarks. Some numbers get better (e.g. +5%), some numbers get worse (e.g. -10%). The same micro-benchmark can get faster on one C compiler but slower on another There's a fundamental disconnect that makes it difficult for humans to reason about performance in computer programs. Because the speed of light is so slow, computer architecture as we know it will always rely on cache and OoO to be fast. The human brain does seem to work out of order, but it's only used to thinking about a world that runs in order. When we use theory of mind, we don't model other people's minds, we use our own as a model for theirs; see mirror neurons[1]. Because of this, standard code benchmarks are not very useful, unless they can demonstrate order-of-magnitude speedups. Even something like a causal profiler[2][3][4], which attempts to control for the volatile aspects of performance, is of limited use; it cannot control for all variables and its results will likely be invalidated by the same architectural variation it tries to control for. Instead (with respect to performance) we should focus on three factors: - Code maintainability - Algorithmic complexity - Cache coherency Everything else is a distraction. 1. [LINK] 2. [VIDEO] 3. [LINK] 4. [LINK]

comments.text: > I originally missed your point about "multiples of" That wasn't my point, but the claim of the poster I was replying to, and it was exactly this claim that I think is unsupportable. Has some software gotten faster? Sure. But mostly software has a gotten slower and the rarer cases of software getting faster have been outpaced significantly by HW. > You want examples where software has sped up at a rate faster than hardware "several multiples": that in some/many areas software has improved performance by several multiples of the improvement in hardware performance over the last 20 years > [JavaScript] JIT compilers have improved The original JITs were done in the late 80s early 90s. And their practical impact is far less then the claimed impact. [LINK] As an example the Cog VM is a JIT for Squeak. They claim a 5x speedup in bytecodes/s. Nice. However the naive bytecode interpreter, in C, on commodity hardware in 1999 (Pentium/400) was 45 times faster than the one microcoded on a Xerox Dorado in 1984, which was a high-end, custom-built ECL machine costing many hundred thousands of dollars. (19m bytecodes/s vs. 400k bytecodes/s). So 5x for software, at least 45x for hardware. And the hardware kept improving afterward, nowadays at least another 10x. > [compilers] Parsing isn't as simple as it seems [..] Parsing is not where the time goes. > 2005-era swift running faster Swift generally has not gotten faster at all. I refer you back to Proebsting's Law and the evidence gathered i
